entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abu'l Hassan Ali ibn Ridwan Al-Misri (died 1061 CE) was an eminent Arab physician, astrologer, and astronomer whose intellectual contributions flourished within the vibrant scientific landscape of Fatimid Egypt. Born in Giza, he became a central figure in the transmission and advancement of Hellenistic scientific thought, particularly through his exhaustive commentary on Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*. His work bridged ancient Greek wisdom with the burgeoning scholarship of the Islamic Golden Age, establishing him as a critical conduit for astrological and medical knowledge that would later influence both the East and the Latin West.

Ibn Ridwan's most significant achievements include his detailed astronomical observations, notably his meticulous description of the supernova SN 1006, which he recorded as a 'large circular body' brighter than Venus, providing one of the most important historical accounts of this stellar event. As a physician, he authored *On the Prevention of Bodily Ills in Egypt*, a treatise that offered early epidemiological insights by correlating environmental factors with public health, advising on sanitation and diet. His medical practice was based in Fustat (Old Cairo), where he served as a prominent figure in the local intellectual community, engaging with contemporary scholarly debates and contributing to the practical application of medicine.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ali ibn Ridwan's meticulous commentary on Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos* and his unique observation of the supernova SN 1006 were critical for the transmission and advancement of Hellenistic astronomical and astrological knowledge. His work significantly influenced both Islamic and later European scholarly traditions, providing a foundational text for centuries.
